Bessent says SEC and CFTC can fill the Clarity Act gap, but agency rules come with an expiry risk
summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Washington can still deliver crypto rules without Congress. Speaking at Ripple’s Swell conference, he said the Senate’s failure to pass the Clarity Act was disappointing, but that Treasury would use its convening power to push a regulatory framework forward through agency action with the SEC and CFTC. The catch for investors is durability: rules written by regulators can be rewritten by the next set of regulators. What happened Bessent described the SEC and CFTC as “great partners” in the effort. He also raised debanking, the practice of financial institutions cutting off services to crypto businesses, sometimes allegedly under regulatory pressure. He said the Clarity Act could have prevented a repeat of that, but that regulatory best practices and protections can still reduce the risk. He also argued that stablecoins will lift demand for the US dollar and Treasuries, making them an important funding source for the government. The backdrop is the Senate vote six weeks ago. The Clarity Act failed to advance on September 15 on a 49-50 vote, 11 short of the 60 needed. Because the vote was procedural, the bill was never debated or amended. The two disputes that sank it were ethics rules covering officials’ digital asset holdings and whether stablecoin issuers can offer yield or rewards. title: US Wholesale inventories 0.6% vs 0.5% estimate
summary: Wholesale inventories: +0.6% MoM. Prior +0.5%, unrevised. Retail inventories: +0.3% MoM. Prior revised to +0.3% from +0.2%. Wholesale inventories: $1,011.5 billion, up 7.4% YoY. Retail inventories: $885.3 billion, up 4.8% YoY. US wholesale inventories rose 0.6% in September, following a 0.5% increase in August, according to the Census Bureau’s advance estimates. Retail inventories increased 0.3%, matching August’s upwardly revised gain. Both wholesale and retail inventories remained above year-earlier levels. The figures are adjusted for seasonal variations and trading day differences, but not for price changes. Quick analysis: Wholesale stockbuilding picked up, while retail inventory growth held steady. Inventories can support gross domestic product (GDP) growth when the pace of accumulation accelerates, but rising stocks can reflect either preparation for stronger sales or unsold goods. Sales data and inflation-adjusted quarterly figures are needed to judge the impact. On their own, these readings offer limited direction for Federal Reserve policy, Treasury yields or the dollar. What this report measures: Advance inventory estimates track the value of goods held by wholesalers and retailers at month-end. These preliminary figures are subject to revision and are not adjusted for inflation. Traders monitor inventories for clues about demand, business activity and their contribution to GDP. This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

This is the first time the sub-index has moved above zero since the start of the US-Iran conflict. However, that optimistic signal is offset by another fall in income expectations. That fell to -15.7 from -15.0 previously, reflecting a modest decline after the slump in the prior month. Meanwhile, price expectations were also seen increasing further to 1.0 - moving back into positive territory. The survey shows that consumers are again expecting somewhat higher inflation, especially after consumer prices rose to 3.3% in September amid higher fuel prices. GfK notes that: "Consumers are looking increasingly optimistic at economic developments but when it comes to their own wallets, skepticism still prevails. Growing worries about inflation and subdued income prospects are dampening the willingness to make larger purchases, even if the propensity to save is falling somewhat." In any case, the data here won't do much to change anything for the ECB decision tomorrow. And in looking to December, it just reaffirms the backdrop that the German economy is still showing uneven signs in terms of growth
